finding.headline: At age 68, this household has already passed age 65, so Medicare timing needs a check now.
details: Medicare says that if you delay and do not sign up at age 65, your coverage may be delayed and cost more. The penalty for missing the 7-month enrollment window grows the longer you wait.
Social Security benefits grow for each month you delay past full retirement age, but the increase stops at age 70. Waiting past 70 adds nothing more.

finding.headline: Almost no tax applies to your income now or in retirement.
details: You pay no tax while you work, and about $4 a year in retirement.
Your savings are all taxable or cash, so they are drawn first, and that is where the plan starts.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice; a tax professional can check the details for you.

plan.verdict_words: falls short: the basics are not safe
assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
You already get Social Security (from 68): the plan uses the $17,000 a year you gave.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 92. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
